title: What Will Happen To The Gang Next Year?

jokes.text: You didn't whisper in my ear and kiss me to wake me up like you always do. / I've never done that.
jokes.setup: Liz complains that Criss didn't do his romantic morning ritual of whispering and kissing her awake
jokes.punchline: Criss flatly denies having ever done this, suggesting Liz dreamed or fabricated the whole romantic tradition
jokes.explanation: Sharp cold open joke. The setup implies a sweet romantic gesture; the punchline instantly deflates it by revealing it never happened — Liz has been imagining or dreaming a tenderness that doesn't exist. Good economy and deadpan delivery implied. Characterizes both Liz's romantic self-delusion and Criss's bluntness efficiently.

jokes.text: You named your van after the guy from Dawson's Creek? / I've seen everything he's ever been in except for that.
jokes.setup: Liz asks if Criss named his van 'Van Der Beek' after the Dawson's Creek actor
jokes.punchline: Criss has seen everything James Van Der Beek has ever done EXCEPT the show he's most famous for — a perfectly absurd fan devotion with a gaping hole
jokes.explanation: Excellent compact joke. The misdirection is that a Van Der Beek superfan would obviously have seen Dawson's Creek. The inversion — he's seen everything BUT that — is a perfectly illogical but internally consistent character quirk. The economy is exceptional; the joke lands in one line.

jokes.text: I am still watching Smash, Criss.
jokes.setup: Criss accuses Liz of being someone who bails; Liz defends her loyalty
jokes.punchline: Her evidence that she doesn't bail is that she's still watching the critically-derided NBC show Smash — a self-deprecating meta-joke about NBC's own terrible programming
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. It functions on three levels: (1) character joke about Liz's stubbornness/loyalty being applied to mundane things, (2) meta-joke where NBC's 30 Rock mocks NBC's own terrible show Smash, and (3) the extreme economy — five words do enormous comedic work. The character_integration is near-perfect: only Liz Lemon would cite still watching a bad TV show as proof of her reliability. Justifies 8+ because of layered wit and cultural resonance.

jokes.text: Fine, I'll go first. Since I had to move out of Razmig's place, my living situation's been a little in flux, and obviously I can't go to a homeless shelter. I mean, the people there can be a little sexually conservative for my tastes.
jokes.setup: Hazel announces 'girl talk time' and says she'll go first as if this is a mutual sharing session
jokes.punchline: She dismisses homeless shelters not out of pride but because the people there are 'sexually conservative' — an absurd inversion of expected objections to homelessness
jokes.explanation: Strong character joke — Hazel's rejection of the homeless shelter for sexual reasons is a perfect encapsulation of her depraved priorities. The misdirection works well: the expected complaint would be dignity or safety. Good character integration for a recurring gag type on 30 Rock.

jokes.text: Can't hack it in the big city? Gonna move to the bay area now, pretend that that was your dream the whole time? Have fun always carrying a light sweater.
jokes.setup: Jenna refuses to let Hazel move in and tries to set a boundary
jokes.punchline: Hazel pivots to a weirdly specific and accurate mockery of people who move to San Francisco — 'always carrying a light sweater' is an unexpectedly precise geographic burn
jokes.explanation: The Bay Area joke is a sharp observational turn — 'pretend that was your dream the whole time' is a real cultural truth about people who move there, and 'always carrying a light sweater' is a hyper-specific punchline that rewards attention. Good but not exceptional.

jokes.text: I look forward to reading your obituary, 'Least famous person in the world dies.'
jokes.setup: Jenna dismisses Hazel and says goodbye
jokes.punchline: Jenna's parting shot imagines Hazel's obituary headline — perfectly capturing Jenna's obsession with fame as the only metric of human value
jokes.explanation: Strong Jenna joke. The mock obituary format is sharp, and 'Least famous person in the world dies' is both a believable Jenna insult and a funny concept in itself. The character integration is excellent — this specific vanity-based cruelty is pure Jenna Maroney.

jokes.text: Lemon, didn't you get ordained online and perform a lesbian wedding last summer? / Yes, I married Becky and Dee because love is love and there's no reason they shouldn't experience the joy of marriage like any other couple. / I'm not going to the container store. This is my Saturday.
jokes.setup: Jack asks if Liz is ordained; Liz launches into a passionate defense of marriage equality
jokes.punchline: She preemptively refuses to go to the Container Store before Jack can even ask — revealing her political speech was just defensive positioning against a mundane errand
jokes.explanation: Excellent misdirection — Liz's heartfelt equality speech is immediately deflated by the reveal that she thought Jack was asking her to run errands. Characterizes Liz perfectly: genuinely liberal but also perpetually on guard against being used. The Container Store specificity elevates it.

jokes.text: You just turned into your father.
jokes.setup: Liz says 'Congratulations' to Jack for getting her to agree to officiate
jokes.punchline: Jack dryly notes she's become her father — presumably a judgmental, reluctant type — by just saying 'congratulations' dismissively
jokes.explanation: Competent one-liner. Jack's 'you just turned into your father' is quick and cutting but relies on an established pattern without a specific twist. Functional but not memorable.

jokes.text: What Bill O'Reilly erotic novel are you living in?
jokes.setup: Jack says both Avery and Diana are 'fine' with him kissing Avery's mother
jokes.punchline: Liz's response invokes the real-life Bill O'Reilly sex scandal (he wrote an erotic novel) as the only fictional universe where that scenario would be acceptable
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. References the real Bill O'Reilly's actual erotic novel ('Those Who Trespass') — a specific, earned pop culture reference that rewards savvy viewers. The framing as an 'erotic novel you're living in' is a fresh and witty construction. High quotability, sharp economy, and the character integration works (Liz as the moral voice using absurdist pop culture to make her point). Justifies 8+ because the joke is both specific and structurally elegant.

jokes.text: I suppose our situation is most reminiscent of 'The Commodore's Lust' from the 'Patriot's After Dark' series.
jokes.setup: Liz asks what erotic novel Jack thinks he's living in
jokes.punchline: Jack has a ready answer — a specific fake erotic novel series — implying he knows this genre intimately and has categorized his own life within it
jokes.explanation: Strong callback and character joke. Jack's knowledge of — and identification with — patriot-themed erotica is perfectly on-brand for his patrician, self-serious persona. The fake book title is well-constructed.

jokes.text: I get your Yankees tickets on A-Rod bobblehead day. / And I'm gonna throw that thing in front of a train. / Go Phillies!
jokes.setup: Liz negotiates for Yankees tickets as payment for officiating
jokes.punchline: She announces she'll throw the A-Rod bobblehead in front of a train, then yells 'Go Phillies!' — establishing she's a Phillies fan doing this specifically to torment Jack
jokes.explanation: Solid escalating joke. The request for Yankees tickets is normal; the plan to destroy the bobblehead before a train is satisfyingly unhinged; 'Go Phillies!' lands the character beat. Good but relies on sports knowledge for full impact.

jokes.text: Stop, drop, and roll! Let me out! Let me out!
jokes.setup: The awkward multi-party nervous laughter scene
jokes.punchline: Someone screams fire safety instructions and demands to be let out — a completely non-sequitur panic response to the social situation
jokes.explanation: Weakly attributed absurdist gag. Without visual context, the 'stop drop and roll' line feels random rather than earned. It's not clear who says it or why, which undercuts the comedy. Possibly funnier in context with performance.

jokes.text: You were named 'Man of the Year' by the 'Journal of the Aryan Patriot Party.'
jokes.setup: Dotcom says Tracy should be proud of being named Man of the Year
jokes.punchline: The award is from the Journal of the Aryan Patriot Party — a white supremacist publication honoring a Black man, which is both absurd and a pointed comment on Tracy's public image
jokes.explanation: Sharp dark comedy. The reveal of the Aryan Patriot Party as the source of Tracy's award is an excellent misdirection that simultaneously comments on Tracy's chaotic public persona. The absurdity is well-earned by the setup.

jokes.text: Did they say when the banquet is? Because I'm kind of between tuxes due to weight fluctuation.
jokes.setup: Dotcom is horrified that Tracy was named Man of the Year by a white supremacist group
jokes.punchline: Tracy's response is to ask about the banquet and worry about his tux fitting — completely missing the moral horror and focused only on the logistics of attending
jokes.explanation: Excellent Tracy character joke. His response is perfectly in-character — oblivious to the political scandal, focused only on personal logistics. 'Between tuxes due to weight fluctuation' is a great specific detail. The deadpan delivery of the absurd is Tracy Jordan at his best.

jokes.text: For instance, in Pixar's upcoming movie about trash, I'm doing the voice of a lazy bottle of grape-flavored soda named Funky Bobo.
jokes.setup: Dotcom says Tracy is a representative of the Black community and should be making them look better
jokes.punchline: Tracy cites his upcoming Pixar role — a 'lazy bottle of grape-flavored soda named Funky Bobo' — as evidence he's improving Black representation
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Every word of 'lazy bottle of grape-flavored soda named Funky Bobo' is load-bearing comedy — the specificity is devastating. Tracy cites this as a proud achievement while Dotcom stares in disbelief. The character integration is exceptional: only Tracy Jordan would sincerely present this as positive representation. The 'Okay, I hear it!' callback lands perfectly. Justifies 8+ on all dimensions.

jokes.text: Okay, I hear it!
jokes.setup: Tracy finishes explaining that 'Funky Bobo' is a lazy grape soda named character
jokes.punchline: He immediately acknowledges the problem himself — a self-aware beat that shows Tracy has a half-second of clarity before returning to his worldview
jokes.explanation: Perfect three-word topper on the Funky Bobo joke. Tracy's brief self-awareness before pivoting back to his worldview is great character comedy. Economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: Scott and I saw each other every day at work, but we're forbidden from speaking. / I was living in an exact replica of Cinderella's castle that Kim Jong-Un had built for his shoe collection. / And I was kept in a pit where they made me beat my best friend to death.
jokes.setup: Avery and Scott describe their time as North Korean captives
jokes.punchline: The details escalate absurdly — Cinderella's castle for shoes, being kept in a pit, beating a best friend to death — played with the matter-of-fact tone of a morning news segment
jokes.explanation: The escalating absurdity of North Korean imprisonment details is well-executed. The deadpan contrast between the horrors described and the casual morning show framing is where the comedy lives.

jokes.text: Awkward. / Wow. What an ordeal. / And I know a little bit about suffering because I work out... A lot! / I think we have a clip.
jokes.setup: Guests describe being forced to beat their best friend to death in a North Korean pit
jokes.punchline: The host says 'Awkward,' then equates that suffering with her own workout regimen, then immediately pivots to a clip — a grotesque compression of genuine horror into morning show triviality
jokes.explanation: Sharp media satire. The host's self-insertion ('I work out a lot') and rapid pivot to 'I think we have a clip' after hearing about torture is excellent observational comedy about morning show culture. The 'Awkward' opener is a nice touch of millennial-speak in a corporate media context.

jokes.text: The slow-reveal clip of Avery and Scott's news broadcast where they tap a coded message to each other, with Kim Jong-Un winning Miss Universe mentioned in passing.
jokes.setup: The morning show says they have a clip of the North Korean news broadcast
jokes.punchline: Kim Jong-Un has won his 'fifth Miss Universe title in four years' — a completely throwaway absurdist detail in the news ticker, while the 'real' story is the tapping code
jokes.explanation: The Kim Jong-Un Miss Universe detail is an excellent throwaway absurdist gag — the kind of joke 30 Rock hides in the background. Rewatch bonus because viewers will catch different layers on repeat viewing.

jokes.text: The repeated rewinding of the broadcast as Avery keeps saying Scott's name with increasing feeling while Scott tries to complete the sports highlight, and the audience decodes 'It's a code!'
jokes.setup: Clip shows Avery saying 'Thank you, Scott Scottsman' and Scott struggling to give sports highlights while she emotionally repeats his name
jokes.punchline: The clip rewinds three times, each time Avery's 'Thank you, Avery' from Scott becoming more loaded, until the host exclaims 'It's a code!' — the comedy escalates through repetition
jokes.explanation: Well-structured running gag. The comedy comes from the rewinding building tension, and the 'It's a code!' payoff is satisfying. Scott's name 'Scott Scottsman' is also a quietly funny background joke.

jokes.text: I was gonna come in here and cry 'cause I didn't get back into the page program. But instead I'm being brave.
jokes.setup: Hazel enters Kenneth's space
jokes.punchline: She announces she was going to cry but is 'being brave' — performing bravery in the least brave possible way by narrating it out loud to get sympathy
jokes.explanation: Decent character beat. Hazel's performative bravery is consistent with her manipulative personality. The joke is that announcing bravery undermines it.

jokes.text: I'll have to go back upstate to that cult. Oh, God, I had so many husbands.
jokes.setup: Hazel says she has nowhere to live
jokes.punchline: She'd have to return to her upstate cult, and her complaint about it is specifically that she had 'so many husbands' there — a darkly funny detail that implies polygamous cult life was exhausting
jokes.explanation: Sharp dark joke. The callback to Hazel's cult background is good, and 'I had so many husbands' as the specific complaint (not the abuse or control, but the quantity of husbands) is a perfect character reveal. Economy is strong.

jokes.text: Well, where will you sit patiently in the dark while you wait for the next day to start? I mean, sleep?
jokes.setup: Kenneth asks Hazel where she'll sleep
jokes.punchline: His description of sleep — sitting patiently in the dark waiting for the next day to start — reveals Kenneth's alien, possibly non-human relationship with sleeping, then he self-corrects to the normal word
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke and one of the episode's best. Kenneth's description of sleep as 'sitting patiently in the dark while you wait for the next day to start' is a beautiful piece of character-specific absurdism — it feeds the running series mythology that Kenneth is immortal/inhuman. The self-correction ('I mean, sleep?') is perfectly timed. This is exactly the kind of joke that justifies 30 Rock's reputation for density and craft. Justifies 8+ as it's both a great standalone joke and a deep character moment.

jokes.text: Have a good day, Doris. / [High-pitched] 'You have a good day too, Kenneth.' / Whatever, Doris. Grow up.
jokes.setup: Kenneth says goodbye to someone named Doris before agreeing to let Hazel stay
jokes.punchline: Kenneth does both voices in a high-pitched squeak for 'Doris' and then scolds his imaginary friend/puppet/roommate to 'grow up' — implying Doris is a doll or imaginary companion
jokes.explanation: Excellent visual comedy inferred from transcript. Kenneth clearly has an imaginary friend or doll named Doris that he argues with. The high-pitched voice for Doris, followed by 'Whatever, Doris. Grow up.' is peak Kenneth character comedy — innocent, alien, slightly unnerving. Character integration is exceptional. Justifies 8+ as a great piece of sustained character absurdism.

jokes.text: Ah, so... How was your day? [Long pause — 07 seconds until next line]
jokes.setup: Jack and Avery are home together after her return from North Korea
jokes.punchline: Jack's opener is 'how was your day?' — an absurdly mundane question to someone who was just held captive in North Korea, followed by a long pause that implies neither knows what to say
jokes.explanation: The awkward mundanity of 'how was your day' after North Korean captivity is a well-deployed cringe beat. The silence amplifies the comedy of two overly composed people unable to process their situation.

jokes.text: You love wet feet?
jokes.setup: Jack has been trying to decode Avery's message and thinks he's interpreted her wet feet photo as a coded message of love
jokes.punchline: His sincere attempt at code-breaking lands on 'you love wet feet' — an absurd misread of what was presumably a romantic signal
jokes.explanation: Quick absurdist gag. The economy is excellent — 'you love wet feet?' as a sincere question does a lot with four words. The image is funny in its specificity.

jokes.text: "I miss you at night. I think about you all the time. I couldn't get through this without you. Check out Kim Jong-Un's pants. Where's the flood?"
jokes.setup: Jack reads out what he believes is Avery's coded love message to Scott
jokes.punchline: The message transitions from heartfelt romantic declarations to a sudden, absurd commentary on Kim Jong-Un's high-water pants — a perfect tonal whiplash
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. The romantic letter format lulls you into expecting a conventional jealousy scene, then 'Check out Kim Jong-Un's pants. Where's the flood?' utterly derails it. The specificity of the pants joke (high-water pants in a North Korean context) makes it land. Justifies 8 for structural elegance and the whiplash surprise.

jokes.text: [Raises voice] I'm not even angry anymore! / Nor am I! / Do you wanna watch Downton Abbey tonight? / I'd love to! Maggie Smith is a treasure!
jokes.setup: Jack and Avery have been fighting about her emotional connection to Scott
jokes.punchline: They both announce they're not angry anymore (while clearly still angry, given they're shouting), then immediately pivot to Downton Abbey — two hypercompetent WASPs who refuse to process emotions and pretend the fight is over
jokes.explanation: Strong character comedy. The joke is that they're shouting 'I'm not even angry!' while clearly still processing conflict, then defuse with Downton Abbey — both WASPs suppressing real emotion through cultural refinement. 'Maggie Smith is a treasure!' as a punctuation mark is perfect.

jokes.text: I had no idea the Shmuley Israel Memorial Parade was a predominantly Jewish event.
jokes.setup: Criss calls Liz from the parade where he's selling hot dogs
jokes.punchline: He's shocked to discover that a parade named 'Shmuley Israel Memorial Parade' has a predominantly Jewish crowd — the specificity of the name makes his ignorance absurdly funny
jokes.explanation: Very strong joke. The name 'Shmuley Israel Memorial Parade' is loaded with obvious Jewish indicators, making Criss's shock that it's 'predominantly Jewish' a perfectly calibrated joke about oblivious gentiles. The economy and structure are excellent — the whole joke is in the name vs. the reaction.

jokes.text: You know what kind of women in their 40s have never been married, Liz? Uggos, crazies, and bailers. You're not an uggo. And you're 'ha-ha' crazy, not 'oh, boy' crazy, which means you bail.
jokes.setup: Criss is trying to convince Liz he won't give up on making money for their renovation
jokes.punchline: His taxonomy of unmarried 40s women — Uggos, Crazies, and Bailers — leads to the logical assessment that Liz is 'ha-ha crazy' not 'oh boy crazy' and therefore a Bailer, which is his actual concern
jokes.explanation: Strong joke with an excellent internal structure. The three-category taxonomy is funny on its own, but the sub-categorization of crazy into 'ha-ha crazy' vs. 'oh boy crazy' is the real gem — specific enough to feel true, absurd enough to be funny. The logic is airtight and the delivery implies it's meant as a compliment. Justifies 8 for structural elegance and quotability.

jokes.text: Planty, no! / I don't care about that.
jokes.setup: Liz and Criss are talking about having a baby/plant
jokes.punchline: Liz suddenly cries out to 'Planty' — presumably a plant she's watching — and Criss dismisses whatever disaster just happened with 'I don't care about that,' staying focused on the emotional conversation
jokes.explanation: Quick physical comedy beat, funny in context — Liz's maternal anxiety manifesting toward a plant mid-phone call. The joke is that it interrupts a sincere moment and Criss doesn't even engage with it.

jokes.text: Hazel does an impression of Kenneth for Jenna — gasping, snorting, groaning. Jenna calls out 'Doris!'
jokes.setup: Hazel performs an impression of Kenneth to Jenna.
jokes.punchline: The impression apparently involves gasping, snorting, and groaning sounds — and Jenna names it 'Doris,' suggesting Hazel's Kenneth impression looks like someone else entirely.
jokes.explanation: The callback to Doris is well-earned, and the physical impression (inferred from sound effects) plays well. Somewhat dependent on visual performance, so loses impact in transcript-only reading.

jokes.text: I'd admire you if you weren't brunette.
jokes.setup: Jenna confronts Hazel and says she knows how Hazel thinks — she lies, cheats, manipulates
jokes.punchline: Jenna qualifies her admiration for Hazel's manipulative skill with the caveat that she can't fully respect a brunette — a perfect encapsulation of Jenna's vanity overriding everything else
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Jenna joke. The punchline pivot from genuine confrontation to shallow hair-color prejudice is perfect — and it's exactly what Jenna would say. The economy is superb: one clause does complete character work. Justifies 8+ for character integration and economy. Jenna's shallowness subverting the drama of the scene is quintessential 30 Rock.

jokes.text: I'm a natural blonde. / That's insane!
jokes.setup: Jenna says she can't fully admire Hazel because she's brunette
jokes.punchline: Hazel claims to be a natural blonde; Jenna's response of 'That's insane!' is both about the obvious lie AND possibly about the idea that a natural blonde would choose to appear brunette
jokes.explanation: Good quick topper on the blonde/brunette exchange. Jenna's 'That's insane!' is a well-timed deadpan reaction that works on multiple levels.

jokes.text: Stop looking at my ass. / Stop pointing your ass at my eyeballs.
characters: Two characters — likely Tracy and Dotcom or Tracy and Cornel West
jokes.setup: One character tells another to stop looking at their butt
jokes.punchline: The response reframes the offense as the first character's fault for positioning their ass at eye level — a perfectly calibrated blame-reversal
jokes.explanation: Sharp physical comedy exchange. 'Stop pointing your ass at my eyeballs' is a great line — the phrasing ('at my eyeballs') is specific and funny, and the blame-reversal logic is absurd but airtight. Good economy.

jokes.text: It's an honor to finally meet you, Questlove. / Tracy, this is Dr. Cornel West.
jokes.setup: Tracy is introduced to Dr. Cornel West
jokes.punchline: Tracy thinks he's meeting Questlove (the drummer from The Roots) — presumably because both have large Afros — requiring Dotcom to correct him
jokes.explanation: Good character joke. Tracy confusing a prominent Black intellectual with a famous musician based on hair is consistent with his character's obliviousness and lack of cultural context. The confusion itself comments on the episode's theme about Black representation.

jokes.text: Darth Vader, ninjas, some black licorice I tried to make into the shape of my dad.
jokes.setup: Dr. Cornel West asks Tracy who his Black role models were growing up
jokes.punchline: Tracy's list of 'Black role models' includes Darth Vader (Black voice, white face), ninjas (Japanese), and a piece of licorice he shaped into his absent father — absurd, sad, and hilarious simultaneously
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. Tracy's 'Black role models' list operates on multiple levels simultaneously: (1) Pure comedy from the absurd choices (ninjas, Darth Vader), (2) The escalating tragedy of 'some black licorice I tried to make into the shape of my dad' — a deeply sad detail about an absent father wrapped in absurdity, (3) Perfect character integration — only Tracy Jordan has this specific background, (4) The licorice joke is both funny and genuinely affecting, which is the highest achievement in comedy writing. Comparable to the 'Snip snap snip snap' anchor in its ability to be both funny and emotionally resonant. Justifies 9+ in all categories.

jokes.text: But where should I look? / Might be closer than you think. Maybe right under your own nose. / Under my own nose. Like a mustache. A mustache. Tom Selleck!
jokes.setup: Cornel West gives Tracy a meaningful metaphor about looking for role models 'right under your own nose'
jokes.punchline: Tracy takes the metaphor completely literally — 'under my own nose' = mustache = Tom Selleck — jumping to an absurd but internally logical conclusion
jokes.explanation: Superb joke. The literal-vs.-metaphorical misread is a classic comedy structure, but 'Tom Selleck' as the specific, logical-to-Tracy conclusion is perfect. The chain of reasoning (under nose → mustache → Tom Selleck) is both absurd and airtight. Excellent character integration — Tracy's literalism is his defining trait. Justifies 8+ for structure and the precision of the Selleck punchline.

jokes.text: You've got to go to a civil rights museum. / I'm praying for my brother.
jokes.setup: Tracy announces Tom Selleck as his role model after Cornel West tried to inspire him
jokes.punchline: West abandons the intellectual approach and tells Tracy to go to a civil rights museum (the last resort), then says 'I'm praying for my brother' — giving up on Tracy entirely
jokes.explanation: Good button on the scene. West's exasperated pivot to 'just go to a museum' and then his prayerful resignation is a satisfying payoff. The joke is that Tracy has defeated a Princeton professor.

jokes.text: I'm praying for my brother. [Cornel West's reaction after Tracy misses the point entirely and runs off to find Tom Selleck]
jokes.setup: Cornel West has tried to impart wisdom to Tracy; Tracy has concluded his role model is Tom Selleck.
jokes.punchline: West's measured, sad declaration — 'I'm praying for my brother' — is both sincere and comedically resigned. The full weight of failed mentorship in five words.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the Tom Selleck sequence. West's resignation is the ideal reaction beat — not anger, not confusion, just quiet prayer. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Diana! The ceremony's not for a little while. You might wanna pace yourself.
jokes.setup: Diana appears to already be drinking before the vow renewal ceremony
jokes.punchline: Liz's 'pace yourself' implies Diana is already drunk at an early hour — the understatement of 'not for a little while' doing the work
jokes.explanation: Functional joke establishing Diana's drinking. Competent but not particularly inventive — the 'pace yourself' gag is a standard comedy beat for drunk characters.

jokes.text: One day we made love while tapping. It was beautiful. No butt stuff.
jokes.setup: Scott explains his relationship with Avery — they tapped secret messages to each other during North Korean news broadcasts
jokes.punchline: He volunteers that their Morse-code-lovemaking was 'beautiful' and then proactively clarifies 'No butt stuff' — an unasked-for denial that makes the situation significantly weirder
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. 'We made love while tapping' is already absurd and funny. 'No butt stuff' — volunteered without any prompting — is a perfect escalation. The unprompted disclaimer implies he felt he needed to say it, which is funnier than any follow-up could be. High quotability. Justifies 8+ for the spontaneous, unprompted nature of the clarification being funnier than the setup.

jokes.text: Jack and Nancy. / No, do not do anything.
jokes.setup: Liz is trying to keep track of who is in love with whom and mixing up all of Jack's women
jokes.punchline: She accidentally says 'Nancy' (a previous Jack girlfriend) instead of 'Avery' — revealing how many women Jack has cycled through that Liz can't keep track
jokes.explanation: Good running gag callback for longtime viewers who remember Nancy Donovan. The comedy is in Liz's exasperated confusion about Jack's relationship history. Works better with series knowledge.

jokes.text: Kim Jong-Il is dead. I'm only waiter. I'm greatest waiter of all time.
jokes.setup: Liz assumes the waiter asking about the 'speak now' vows is a North Korean agent
jokes.punchline: The waiter clarifies he's just asking as a waiter, mentions Kim Jong-Il is dead (a non-sequitur) and then declares himself 'the greatest waiter of all time' with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Good absurdist gag. The waiter's combination of a political non-sequitur and grandiose professional self-assessment is a funny non-sequitur. 'I'm greatest waiter of all time' is a great deadpan line.

jokes.text: Three different people independently asking Liz whether she's going to do the 'speak now or forever hold your peace' part of the ceremony.
jokes.setup: Liz is officiating the vow renewal; Diana, then Scott, then the waiter all independently ask her about the 'speak now' portion
jokes.punchline: The third inquiry (from the waiter) makes Liz realize everyone has a reason to object — the running gag escalates to comic inevitability
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural comedy. The triple repetition of the same question from progressively more absurd askers (close family → romantic rival → random waiter) builds to a great comedic escalation. The structure itself is the joke — 30 Rock using sitcom formula self-consciously.

jokes.text: To quote George W. Bush, Lemon, 'bring 'em on.' / He said that to me in Galveston when a busload of drunk debutantes tried to get on his boat. It was named 'Mr. Water Boat.' / Did it sink? Yes. Because there were too many people on it. But the spirit of his words lives on.
jokes.setup: Jack quotes George W. Bush to inspire confidence about his vow renewal
jokes.punchline: Jack has a specific, implausible personal anecdote about Bush that ends with the boat sinking due to too many drunk debutantes — and he treats the lesson as inspirational rather than cautionary
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The anecdote is perfectly Jack Donaghy — wealthy, connected, name-dropping a president from a personal story. The boat named 'Mr. Water Boat' is an absurd detail (implying Bush named it something extremely simple), and the fact that it did sink but 'the spirit lives on' is a great comic non-conclusion. Every element works: character integration, absurdist details, the inspirational framing of a disaster. Justifies 8.5 for the density of good decisions in a short passage.

jokes.text: Oh, are you talking about Hazel or the raccoon that won't let me into my kitchen? Either way, the answer is 'wonderful.'
jokes.setup: Jack asks how things are with Kenneth's new roommate
jokes.punchline: Kenneth has both a new human roommate AND a raccoon that has taken over his kitchen, and he responds to both with cheerful 'wonderful' — unable to recognize either as a problem
jokes.explanation: Excellent Kenneth joke. The raccoon is a perfect absurdist detail — Kenneth's apartment apparently has a raccoon that controls his kitchen, and this is presented as equivalent to the Hazel situation. His inability to distinguish problems from blessings ('either way, wonderful') is essential Kenneth character comedy. Justifies 8+ for character integration and the raccoon detail being both funny and specific.

jokes.text: This isn't my application. This isn't even my handwriting. / Do you know whose handwriting it is? / Hazel's. / She sabotaged you so you won't become a threat. / And to think I thought Hazel was a bitch!
jokes.setup: Jenna reveals Hazel forged Kenneth's page program application to sabotage him
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's response to learning Hazel is a manipulative saboteur is to say 'And to think I thought Hazel was a bitch!' — implying 'bitch' was a compliment in his mind and this is actually worse
jokes.explanation: Strong joke. Kenneth's innocent misuse of 'bitch' — apparently as a neutral or positive descriptor — is perfectly on-brand, and the reveal that this new information is somehow worse than being a 'bitch' is a great inversion. The character integration is excellent.

jokes.text: Friendly and loyal like a well-trained female dog. But she isn't a bitch. She's a meaniepants.
jokes.setup: Kenneth used 'bitch' as a compliment; now he clarifies what he meant
jokes.punchline: He defines 'bitch' as 'friendly and loyal like a well-trained female dog' and pivots to calling Hazel a 'meaniepants' — the juxtaposition of this grown man's vocabulary is perfect
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's top jokes. Kenneth's sincere, literal definition of 'bitch' (as a dog term) and his pivot to 'meaniepants' as the real insult is extraordinary character comedy. It rewards the setup perfectly, is deeply specific to Kenneth's innocence, and 'meaniepants' is one of the funniest single-word punchlines in the episode. Justifies 8.8 for being almost perfect character-integrated joke writing — every word is essential.

jokes.text: Police are reporting that a bank on Jackson Avenue was robbed this afternoon by a lone suspect — a white male in his 30s. Security cameras caught the getaway van heading West towards Manhattan. / Nerf-herder!
jokes.setup: TV news reports a bank robbery with a getaway van; audience has just seen Criss drive away in his van
jokes.punchline: Liz's reaction — 'Nerf herder!' (a Star Wars insult) — is her immediate conclusion that Criss robbed a bank, expressed in the most Liz Lemon way possible
jokes.explanation: Strong joke. The news report perfectly matches Criss's description, and Liz's use of 'Nerf herder' (a Star Wars insult from Empire Strikes Back — 'you stuck-up, half-witted, scruffy-looking nerf herder') as her expletive of choice is perfect Liz Lemon character comedy. The misdirection works because the audience shares Liz's incorrect conclusion.

jokes.text: What about Frederick Douglass? / A guy with two first names? Next.
jokes.setup: Dotcom is trying to help Tracy find a Black role model at the civil rights museum
jokes.punchline: Tracy dismisses Frederick Douglass because he has two first names — a completely irrelevant criterion that Tracy has apparently pre-established
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. The criterion of 'two first names' as a disqualifier for historical figures is a brilliantly absurd Tracy-logic filter. The economy is perfect — 'A guy with two first names? Next.' is six words that do enormous comedic work. Justifies 8+ for the economy and the perfect character voice.

jokes.text: That dress belonged to Rosa Parks. She's one of my personal heroes. / I think I found my role model. / Good choice. / Shut up, Dotcom. I'm not talking about her. I'm talking about me looking funny in this reflection.
jokes.setup: Tracy is shown Rosa Parks's dress and appears moved; everyone assumes he's found a Black role model
jokes.punchline: He was inspired by himself looking funny in the display case reflection, not Rosa Parks — and his new inspiration is to play a 'fat old aunt' in Tyler Perry-style movies
jokes.explanation: Outstanding joke. The misdirection is beautifully constructed — the pause, the apparent sincerity of 'I think I found my role model,' and then the complete subversion. 'I'm talking about me looking funny in this reflection' is both a perfect Tracy joke AND a meta-commentary on the episode's theme about Black representation and Tyler Perry. The structure is essentially perfect. Justifies 8.6 — one of the episode's best.

jokes.text: I'm gonna do a movie where I play someone's fat old aunt and I say stuff like, 'Whoo-wee!' And 'Sweet child, sit yo' black ass down!'
jokes.setup: Tracy explains his new Tyler Perry-inspired movie plan
jokes.punchline: He enthusiastically describes playing a 'fat old aunt' character — the exact stereotype the episode has been critiquing — as his solution to the problem of Black representation
jokes.explanation: Strong joke that works on the irony that Tracy has learned nothing from the civil rights museum. His solution to the representation problem is to do the most stereotypical thing possible, delivered with full enthusiasm. Good character integration.

jokes.text: You can't go to prison, you idiot. They will ravage you and your beautiful woman face.
jokes.setup: Liz thinks Criss robbed a bank and confronts him
jokes.punchline: Her concern for Criss is that prison inmates will ravage him because of his 'beautiful woman face' — a compliment and a concern at the same time, specific to Criss's conventionally attractive looks
jokes.explanation: Solid joke. 'Beautiful woman face' is a funny and specific description, and the concern that he'll be ravaged for it is both dark and a genuine expression of Liz's affection. Competent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: I can handle prison. I have a mean face and I can will myself to sleep in any environment.
jokes.setup: Liz says she'll go to prison instead of Criss
jokes.punchline: Her prison qualifications — a mean face and the ability to will herself to sleep — are charmingly inadequate and deeply specific to Liz's self-assessment
jokes.explanation: Strong character joke. The two listed prison qualifications are perfectly calibrated for Liz — she genuinely believes these would be sufficient. 'I can will myself to sleep in any environment' as a prison survival skill is both funny and rings true for her character.

jokes.text: I sold the van this morning... to a really nice young guy on meth.
jokes.setup: Criss reveals he didn't rob a bank — he sold the van
jokes.punchline: The buyer is described as 'a really nice young guy on meth' — the 'really nice' sincerity combined with 'on meth' is a perfect dark detail
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy joke. 'A really nice young guy on meth' — the juxtaposition of 'really nice' with 'on meth' is a perfect absurdist combo. The deadpan delivery implied by the transcript makes it land. Very quotable.

jokes.text: You sold Van Der Beek? For me? / I sold Van Der Beek... For us.
jokes.setup: Liz is touched that Criss sold his beloved van
jokes.punchline: The romantic 'for us' pivot on the van's name 'Van Der Beek' — treating the van as a proper named character in their relationship — gives a rom-com emotional beat a sitcom-absurd texture
jokes.explanation: Sweet callback that earns its emotional beat by making the van named 'Van Der Beek' do double duty as both a character and a punchline. The shift from 'for me' to 'for us' is a genuine rom-com moment, but the absurdity of the name keeps it from being saccharine.

jokes.text: I don't wanna wait for our lives to be over.
jokes.setup: Criss declares his commitment to Liz and their future
jokes.punchline: The line is the opening lyric of the Dawson's Creek theme song ('I Don't Want to Wait' by Paula Cole) — a callback to the Van Der Beek joke, and a meta-joke that Criss, who's seen everything Van Der Beek has done EXCEPT Dawson's Creek, is unknowingly quoting it
jokes.explanation: The best structural joke in the episode and among the best callback jokes in 30 Rock's run. The setup was established cold in the opening scene: Criss named his van 'Van Der Beek' but has never seen Dawson's Creek. Now, in an emotional romantic moment, he quotes the Dawson's Creek theme song without realizing it. This is a perfect triple-layered joke: (1) It lands as a sincere romantic statement, (2) It's the Dawson's Creek theme for those who catch it, (3) The irony is that Criss — who has seen everything EXCEPT Dawson's Creek — is unknowingly quoting it. The craft is exceptional because the callback was planted many scenes ago and pays off organically. Justifies 9+ across the board.

jokes.text: Have you ever had a girlfriend willing to Thelma and Louise with you? / No. Never. / But come on, Bonnie and Clyde. Okay, I'm a boy. I'm a boy, Liz.
jokes.setup: Liz proposes they're like Thelma and Louise for being loyal to each other
jokes.punchline: Criss rejects the all-female comparison and suggests Bonnie and Clyde instead — then has to remind Liz that he is male, implying Liz sometimes forgets or doesn't care about his gender
jokes.explanation: Strong character joke. The Thelma and Louise reference works as a Liz character beat (she defaults to female buddy films), and 'I'm a boy, Liz' is a funny and specific beat that characterizes how Liz relates to Criss — sometimes treating him as a gender-neutral partner rather than a boyfriend.

jokes.text: Also, I hear Pippa Middleton couldn't come today because Avery was borrowing her ass.
jokes.setup: Scene transitions to the vow renewal; an unnamed character makes an aside
jokes.punchline: Avery has borrowed Pippa Middleton's famous ass for the occasion — a reference to the royal wedding obsession of the era and a good absurdist body-part joke
jokes.explanation: Decent pop culture gag. The Pippa Middleton joke was timely (royal wedding craze was 2011) and the 'borrowing her ass' construction is funny, but it's a throwaway that doesn't connect to character or theme. Functional.

jokes.text: The 'speak now' moment: Diana, Scott, the waiter, and other objectors all groan — then Scott greets his ex-fiancée Teresa; the waiter leaves because he has a shift.
jokes.setup: Liz asks if anyone objects; the entire room is full of people with objections.
jokes.punchline: All the built-up objectors fail to actually object — Scott is distracted by Teresa, the waiter has to work — collapsing all the ceremony's tension into anticlimax.
jokes.explanation: Well-structured payoff on the running 'speak now' gag — all the objectors fizzle out for mundane reasons, making the elaborate setup a long anticlimax. The structural humor of elaborate setups leading to nothing is executed well.

jokes.text: Great! So no one. / Are you people kidding me? Seriously, no one has anything to say? You're all cowards.
jokes.setup: After the 'speak now or forever hold your peace' moment — several people almost objected but didn't — Liz is relieved
jokes.punchline: Avery immediately breaks down and demands to know why no one objected — she WANTED someone to stop the wedding
jokes.explanation: Strong joke. The twist that Avery wanted objections is the payoff of the running 'speak now' gag, and it recontextualizes the whole ceremony. 'You're all cowards' is a great line. Well-structured character reveal.

jokes.text: I have something to say. / I played Avery Jessup in 'Kidnapped By Danger,' now available on Sega Genesis.
jokes.setup: Avery demands someone speak up; Jenna steps forward as if she has a crucial objection
jokes.punchline: Jenna's 'something to say' is only to plug the TV movie she made about Avery's kidnapping — now available on Sega Genesis (a console from the early 1990s)
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Jenna joke. At a moment of genuine emotional crisis, Jenna uses the 'speak now' opportunity to advertise her own TV movie, and the detail that it's 'available on Sega Genesis' is perfect — both absurdly outdated (Sega Genesis hadn't been relevant for 15+ years) and perfectly Jenna (she'd be proud of any platform). Character integration is nearly perfect. Justifies 8.7 for the specificity, timing, and Jenna being pure Jenna.

jokes.text: I forgot about the TV movie that whitewashed our love story. / I was dating another woman. / And I wasn't ready to get married. / Both: We only did it because... / She was pregnant. / I was pregnant.
jokes.setup: Jack and Avery are simultaneously discovering they're better off divorced and listing reasons the marriage was a mistake
jokes.punchline: They simultaneously admit they only got married because of pregnancy — a darkly funny simultaneous confession that explains and deflates the entire marriage
jokes.explanation: Good structural joke. The simultaneous confession structure is well-executed, and the synchronized 'She was pregnant / I was pregnant' is a satisfying double-punchline. The whitewashing mention is also a quick Jenna callback.

jokes.text: The only thing you're bad at is quitting. I kept my sea monkeys alive for 30 years.
jokes.setup: Jack and Avery recognize they're both too stubborn to quit their marriage.
jokes.punchline: Avery's evidence of her pathological inability to quit is keeping sea monkeys alive for 30 years — an absurdly small achievement elevated to character-defining credential.
jokes.explanation: The sea monkey detail is specific and absurd in the right way — sea monkeys famously die quickly, making 30 years of survival an almost supernaturally stubborn act. Works as a character beat and a standalone joke.

jokes.text: I mean, if we wanted this thing to succeed, why would we ask Liz to officiate? / Because I'm good at blending humor and heart?
jokes.setup: Avery and Jack realize they subconsciously wanted their marriage to fail
jokes.punchline: Avery's 'why would we ask Liz to officiate' implies Liz is a jinx or incompetent; Liz's sincere defense — 'I'm good at blending humor and heart' — is a meta-joke about the show's own description of itself
jokes.explanation: Strong meta-joke. Liz's self-description as someone who 'blends humor and heart' is both her sincere self-defense and 30 Rock describing its own show. The meta-self-referential quality elevates what could be a throwaway line.

jokes.text: I'll always care for you. / We'll split assets and custody equally. / I'll take our friends 'A' through 'L.' / You'll get 'M' through 'Z.' / Liz, divorce us.
jokes.setup: Jack and Avery decide to divorce at the vow renewal
jokes.punchline: They split their friends alphabetically — 'A through L' and 'M through Z' — as if friends are an inventory item, then immediately ask Liz to divorce them
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. The alphabetical friend-splitting is perfectly Jack and Avery — hypercompetent, emotionally detached, approaching the end of a marriage with corporate efficiency. The immediate pivot to 'Liz, divorce us' at a vow renewal is a great structural subversion. Justifies 8+ for character integration and the inventive logic of the alphabetical split.

jokes.text: By the power vested in me by the website instaminister.Estonia, I now pronounce you divorced. / [Laughing] Yeah! Divorce! Whoo!
jokes.setup: Jack and Avery have decided to divorce; Liz is to officiate it
jokes.punchline: The ordination website is 'instaminister.Estonia' — an absurdist specific detail implying the least prestigious online ordination possible, and the crowd celebrates the divorce with cheers
jokes.explanation: Strong absurdist joke. 'instaminister.Estonia' is a great invented detail — Estonia's specificity (not .com, not .org, but the Estonian country-code domain) is perfect. The joyful crowd reaction to the divorce announcement is a good tonal subversion.

jokes.text: This would make a great room for a baby. / You said 'baby' instead of 'plant.' / Now say 'man cave.' / Never!
jokes.setup: Liz and Criss are looking at the renovated upstairs room
jokes.punchline: Liz slips and says 'baby' instead of their euphemism 'plant' — Criss immediately notices and calls it out; then he asks her to say 'man cave' which she refuses
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the plant/baby euphemism. Liz's slip reveals her genuine desire for a baby, and Criss catching it is a sweet moment with a comedy beat. The 'man cave' refusal is a funny gender-politics button.

jokes.text: It's the remote control holder you wanted from SkyMall.
jokes.setup: Jack gives Liz a gift as thanks for officiating; her reaction implies it's something absurd and amazing
jokes.punchline: The gift is a SkyMall remote control holder — confirming both that Liz reads SkyMall and that this is genuinely thrilling to her
jokes.explanation: Good Liz Lemon character joke. SkyMall was the catalog of absurd gadgets sold on airplanes — Liz wanting a remote control holder from it is perfectly on-brand for her practical, uncool sensibility. Jack knowing this about her and gifting it says something about their relationship too.

jokes.text: Because we are thinking about having a baby... Together... That will emerge from my vagina. / Or a Chinese vagina. / Okay.
jokes.setup: Liz excitedly tells Jack she and Criss might have a baby, adding increasingly specific details
jokes.punchline: Jack neutrally suggests 'or a Chinese vagina' (referring to adoption from China) and then just says 'Okay' — the complete absence of reaction to either the biological or adoption option is the joke
jokes.explanation: Good character joke. Liz's oversharing ('from my vagina') and Jack's complete deadpan neutrality to both options is funny. The specificity of 'Chinese vagina' as Jack's adoption suggestion is a bit clunky but Jack's 'Okay' lands well.

jokes.text: I've been, uh... Divorced... twice. Engaged two other times. I'm... a mess.
jokes.setup: Liz asks Jack for advice on having a baby.
jokes.punchline: Jack — the show's alpha-male success figure — summarizes his personal life as 'a mess,' the pause-filled confession undercutting all his usual confidence.
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — Jack's rare moment of self-awareness about his romantic failures. The pauses (inferred) and hedging language make it funny as a deflation of the Jack Donaghy persona. Not the strongest joke but serves emotionally.

jokes.text: But any child would be lucky to have you be the mother it loves then hates for a few years, then loves again, then half-heartedly defends to its spouse, then puts in a home.
jokes.setup: Jack says Liz doesn't need his advice but then starts complimenting her potential as a mother
jokes.punchline: His description of motherhood escalates from love to teenage hatred to ambivalent adult love to being put in a nursing home — a darkly funny but accurate lifecycle of the parent-child relationship delivered as a compliment
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke that works as both comedy and genuine sentiment. The escalating realistic lifecycle of the parent-child relationship, delivered as a heartfelt compliment, is perfect dark comedy. 'Half-heartedly defends to its spouse' and 'then puts in a home' as the denouement of motherhood is both funny and true. The structure is beautiful — it sounds like a blessing but ends in a nursing home. Justifies 8+ for the escalation and the bittersweet truth underneath.

jokes.text: If you decide to have a child, you are going to make an excellent mother... as long as you follow Jack Donaghy's 25 Pillars of Motherhood. Number one: don't overthink the names. Stick to Kings and Queens of England. There will never be a President Ashton or a Dr. Katniss. Or a non-sexually confused Lorne.
jokes.setup: Jack says Liz will be an excellent mother — then immediately qualifies it with 25 rules
jokes.punchline: Pillar #1 is about naming conventions; the specific examples of names to avoid ('President Ashton,' 'Dr. Katniss') are good, and 'non-sexually confused Lorne' is a self-referential joke about NBC's Lorne Michaels
jokes.explanation: Strong joke. 'There will never be a President Ashton or a Dr. Katniss' is sharp pop culture satire, and 'non-sexually confused Lorne' is a meta-joke about Lorne Michaels and possibly the name Lorne in general. The '25 Pillars' setup implies Jack has prepared extensively for this moment, which is great character comedy.

jokes.text: Ah, we had a good time tonight. I wonder what will happen to the gang next season.
jokes.setup: The episode is ending; Tracy addresses the camera
jokes.punchline: Tracy breaks the fourth wall to deliver a meta-commentary on the show's upcoming season — a sitcom character wondering about his own fictional future
jokes.explanation: Good meta-joke. Tracy's fourth-wall break to wonder about 'the gang next season' is quintessential 30 Rock meta-comedy. Sets up the finale monologue sequence well.

jokes.text: Will Liz have a baby? Will Jack become supreme leader of Kabletown? Will Kenneth... No, I don't care!
jokes.setup: Tracy is speculating about the characters' futures in a fake season finale cliffhanger
jokes.punchline: He abandons his speculation about Kenneth mid-sentence with 'No, I don't care!' — breaking both the fourth wall and the premise of caring about his costars
jokes.explanation: Good meta-joke. The sudden abandonment of Kenneth's storyline mid-sentence is funny, and Tracy's 'No, I don't care!' is a great character beat — he genuinely can't sustain interest in someone else.

jokes.text: All I want is Jack and Liz get together. On Friends, it was so satisfying. They do on Cheers, they do on Moonlighting. Everybody do it! Don't overthink it, writers. Whoever you are.
jokes.setup: Tracy is demanding what he wants from next season's storylines
jokes.punchline: He wants Jack and Liz to get together citing sitcom precedents (Friends, Cheers, Moonlighting), then addresses 'the writers, whoever you are' — a direct address to the 30 Rock writing room from a 30 Rock character
jokes.explanation: Excellent meta-finale joke. Tracy addressing 'the writers, whoever you are' is the ultimate fourth-wall break, and his analysis of will-they/won't-they sitcom tropes (Friends, Cheers, Moonlighting) is both accurate and self-aware. '30 Rock commenting on whether its own Jack/Liz relationship should follow sitcom convention' is excellent meta-comedy. Justifies 8+ for the layered self-awareness.

tmdb_overview: Determined to prove his marriage has survived Avery's kidnapping unscathed, Jack asks Liz to officiate their vow renewal. Meanwhile, Criss tries to convince Liz that he's worth sticking around for. Tracy meets with Cornel West to discuss his influence as a black celebrity.
insight: Season finale escalates character chaos into 65 jokes across 42 minutes—near-elite density.
